anatomy.lede: A sea pig is a sea cucumber rebuilt for walking: its tube feet have become legs, its back sprouts tall flexible papillae, and a ring of tentacles at the front shovels up mud.

hotspots.label: Feeding tentacles
hotspots.text: Ten tentacles surround the mouth, their surface deeply folded. They gather mud and fresh detritus from the seafloor.

hotspots.label: Dorsal papilla
hotspots.text: The long projections on the back are papillae. Under the microscope they resemble tube feet, each with a large muscular water canal running through the middle.

hotspots.label: Papillae
hotspots.text: Papillae rise from the upper side of the body, giving the sea pig its odd, horned outline.

hotspots.label: See-through body
hotspots.text: The body is pale and translucent, which is why MBARI calls sea pigs 'see-through sea cucumbers'.

hotspots.label: Walking tube feet
hotspots.text: Six pairs of greatly enlarged tube feet grow from the sides of the body and point downwards for walking, holding the body above the soft mud.

hotspots.label: Juvenile king crab
hotspots.text: A young king crab sheltering underneath. Off central California, 22% of nearly 2,600 sea pigs observed had at least one juvenile crab with them.

body.lede: Very few sea pigs have ever been examined under a microscope. A 2021 study of two animals from Monterey Bay found a body similar to other sea cucumbers — with some surprises.

systems.title: Breathing through its feet?
systems.text: Many sea cucumbers breathe with internal 'respiratory trees', but none was found in sea pigs. The large tube feet may take over the job of gas exchange.

systems.title: Hydraulic limbs
systems.text: Like all echinoderms, sea pigs move their tube feet and papillae with a water vascular system: fluid-filled canals run through the centre of each projection.

systems.title: A picky mud-eater
systems.text: Sea pigs in the Santa Catalina Basin had more freshly settled particles in their guts than in the surrounding mud, suggesting they select food that reached the seafloor within roughly the previous 20 days.

systems.title: A skin full of bacteria
systems.text: In sea pigs from the north-west Pacific, a single newly described bacterium made up 76–99% of the microbes in the body wall, forming clusters on the skin's outer side. Its role is still unknown.

genome.lede: No reference genome for a sea pig has been published. A rough, highly fragmented draft for Scotoplanes globosa was deposited in NCBI in 2023 without an accompanying paper.

findings.title: Mitochondrial genomes
findings.text: The much smaller mitochondrial genome has been fully sequenced for an unnamed Scotoplanes species (2018) and for Scotoplanes clarki (2024).
